Learning C has never been easy. That is why the author, basing himself on his experience  teacher, has put all his efforts into writing a book that is easy to read, progressive in  the  learning  and  with  Many  examples  what  clarify  it  exposed.

The way in which the book has been structured has been, precisely, thinking  do in achieving that goal. The book has been divided into twelve chapters that pre-  laying down the language little by little, starting with the simplest, seeing each  theme in due time, until reaching the end where everything related to the  programming with the C language, with hardly any difficulties. It completes the  study of C with a chapter on dynamic structures and another on algorithms.  mos in common use. The reader will be able to verify at the end of this work that the level of  knowledge  what has  acquired is  high.

The first chapter introduces the reader to the world of C programming.  second chapter presents at once all the elements of language that the  reader will use consistently in the rest of the chapters; therefore, you must simple-  mind to be read by looking at the examples and, for the moment, not to worry too much;  later you can return to it as many times as necessary. The third  chapter presents the general structure of a C program with an example; the reader  You should also read it with one goal: to assimilate what the structure of a program is like.  ma C and what is its sequence of execution, without trying to learn right now  all the concepts that are exposed there. Having read these three chapters, the reader will  It will make clear the stage where it is going to move. From chapter 4 you will start to  learn to program; therefore, the reader must have a little patience until  what  start in this  chapter.

This book has several noteworthy features. It is brief in theory and  abundant  on  examples  (plus  from  250  training  solved),  it  what  you  will do  yet  plus

It is evident that the C language has evolved throughout its history.  Product of this evolution was the C++ language and, finally, the design of a  extensive library of functions for the development of applications with a graphical interface  fica (visual programming). Hence, this book is the first in a collection.  of three books oriented to the development of applications with C/C++. between the three, and  in the order discussed below, they cover the following aspects: programming  tion  with  C  and programming  oriented  to objects  with  C++.

This is the first, C/C++ Programming Course . It covers everything related to  structured programming with C. It also includes various algorithms for use  common as well as developments with dynamic data structures. why the title  C/C++? Because C++ was developed from the C programming language and  with few exceptions it includes C. This part of C included in C++ is known  as C–, and could be compiled under C++ without problems. However, when C++  it is used for what it was intended, to perform object-oriented programming.  jets,  the  knowledge  new  what  there are  what  acquire  They are  substantial.

The C language was born in AT&T's Bell Labs and has been closely  associated with the UNIX operating system, since its development was carried out in this  system and because both UNIX and the C compiler itself and the almost totality  Most UNIX programs and tools were written in C. Their efficiency  and clarity have meant that assembly language has hardly been used in  UNIX.

This language is inspired by language B written by Ken Thompson in  1970 with the intention of recoding UNIX, which in the boot phase was written  in assembler, in view of its portability to other machines. B was a len-  evolved and machine-independent language, inspired by the BCPL language  conceived  by  Martin  Richard in 1967.

In 1972, Dennis Ritchie takes over and modifies language B, creating the  C language and rewriting UNIX in that language. The novelty it provided  the  language  C  on  the  B.  was  the  design  from  types  and  structures  from  data.

Likewise, C allows you to work with  addresses  from  memory,  with  functions  and  supports  the  recursion.

### Language  C++

C++ was developed from the C programming language and, with few exceptions,  tions, includes C. This part of C included in C++ is known as C–, and can  from  compile as C++  without  problems.

In 1980, features such as classes (concept  taken from Simula 67), check the type of the arguments of a function and  conversion, if necessary, of the same, as well as other characteristics; the result-  ted  was  the language  called  C  with classes.

In 1983/84, C with Classes was redesigned, extended, and again implemented.  mentioned. The result was called the C++ Language . The main extensions  They were  functions  virtual,  functions  overloaded  (a  same  identifier  can be used to call different forms of a function) and operators on  breloaded  (a  same  operator  can  be used  on  different  contexts  and  with

different meanings). After some further refinement, C++ became available.  available in 1985\. This language was created by Bjarne Stroustrup (AT&T Bell La-  boratories)  and  documented in  some books  his.

The name of C++ is due to Rick Mascitti , meaning the evolutionary character  from  the  transformations of  C  ("++"  is  the  operator  from  increase  from  C).

Subsequently, C++ has been extensively revised and refined, which has given  place to add new features, such as multiple inheritance, member functions  static and const, protected members, generic data types (also called  two templates) and exception handling. In addition to this, there have also  done  little ones  changes  for  increase  the  compatibility  with  c.

### LITERAL

A  literal  is  the  expression  from  a  value  from  a  type  primitive,  or  well  from  a  chain  character (set of characters enclosed in double quotes). For example, they are lit-  rails:  5 ,  3.14 ,  'a' and  "hello" .  Actually  They are  constant values.

As stated, a literal in C can be: an integer, a real, a character and  a  character string.

### literals  integers

The  language  C  It allows  specify  a  literal  whole  on  base  10,  8  and  16.

In general, the + sign is optional if the value is positive and the   sign  will be  present as long as the value is negative. The type of an integer literal depends on  his  base,  from  his  value  and  from  his  suffix.  The  syntax  for  specify  a  literal  whole  is:

{[+]|    }integer_literal[{L|U|UL}]

If the literal is decimal and has no suffix, its type is the first of the int types,  long  int  or  unsigned  long  int  on  the  what  his  value  can  be  represented.

If it is octal or hexadecimal and has no suffix, its type is the first of the types  int, unsigned int, long int, or unsigned long int in which its value can be re-  presented.

You can also explicitly indicate the type of an integer literal, by adding  do  the suffixes L ,  U or UL (uppercase  or lowercase).

If the suffix is L , its type is long when the value can be represented in is-  tea  type;  Yes  no,  is  unsigned  length  Yes  the  suffix  is  U ,  his  type  is  unsigned  int  when

the value  can  be  represented  in this type; if it's not  unsigned long. If the suffix  is UL ,  its type  is  unsigned  length

A decimal integer literal can have one or more digits from 0 to 9 , of which four  them  the  first of  they are  different from  0 . By  example:

4326 constant  whole  int

1522U constant  whole  unsigned  int  1000L constant  whole  long

325UL constant  whole  unsigned  long

A  literal  whole  octal  can  have  one  or  plus  digits  from 0  to  7 ,  preceded  by

0326 constant  whole  int  on  base  8

A hexadecimal integer literal can have one or more digits from 0 to 9 and letters  A through F ( uppercase or lowercase) preceded by 0x or 0X ( zero se-  guide  of x ). For example:

# ENTRY  AND  EXIT  STANDARD

![](Images/image18506.jpeg)

When a program is executed, there are basically three things going on: input  from  the  data,  process  from  the  themselves  and  Exit  or  presentation  from  the  results.

![](Images/image18507.jpeg)

The input task obtains the data needed by the program from some  external medium (for example, from the keyboard or from a file on disk) and stores them  in the computer's memory to be processed; by default the middle of  where  are obtained  is he  keyboard. By  example:

scanf("%g  %g",  &to,  &b);  //  read  to  and  b  from  the  keyboard

The processing of the data will give rise to results that will be stored  temporarily  In Memory.  For example:

c  =  to  +  b;  //  Add  to  and  b;  the  result  I know  stores  on  c

The output task sends the obtained results to another place; for example, the  displays them on the monitor, writes them to the printer, or saves them to a file on  disk. The output operation does not delete data from memory or change the shape  in which they are stored. It simply makes a copy of them to en-  see them  to the  place  specified;  by  omission,  East  place  is  the  screen.  By  example:

printf("%g\n",  c);  //  show  the  result

In this chapter we will study the functions of the C library that allow  have  perform  operations  from  entry  and  from  Exit  (IS)  on  the  devices  is it so-

give from the computer; that is, functions to enter data from the keyboard and functions  tions  to visualize  data in  the screen.

### DATA  NUMERICAL  AND  CHAINS  FROM  CHARACTERS

The purpose of an application is to process data, which will generally be obtained  nested from some external means by the application itself, to obtain results  two.  These  data  and  results  they will be  usually  from  Some  from  these  types:  numeric  or chains of  characters .

Likewise, both the data read and the results obtained will be stored.  stored in variables declared in the functions that make up the program. The  data will be read and/or written through the I/O functions provided by  the C library and will be assigned to variables using a statement  assignment  from the way:

variable  assignment_operator  value

An assignment statement is asymmetric. This means that it evaluates the  expression on the right and the result is assigned to the variable specified on the left.  love.  By  example:

d  =  to  +  b*  c;  //  the  value  from  to  +  b  *  c  I know  assign  to d

But  no  would  valid  to write:

to  +  b  *  c =  d;  //  the  value  from  d  no  I know  can  to assign  to  to  +  b*  c

The numerical data will be stored in variables of one of the types  primitives  exposed  at  chapter  2\. by  example:

double  radio,  area;

//  ...

area  =  3.141592  *  radio  *  radio;

Character strings will be stored in arrays, the study of which has been  postponed  for a later chapter.

When a value is assigned to a variable we are placing that value in a  location  from  memory  associated with that  variable.

int  nvar  =  10; //  variable  from  a  type  primitive  (int)

![](Images/image18508.jpeg)

Logically, when the variable is assigned a value and one is assigned  new, the previous value is destroyed since the new value occupies the same  memory location. In the example below, it can be seen with respect to  to  the  situation  previous,  what  the  contents  from  nvar  I know  modifies  with  a  new  value.

nvar  =  twenty;

![](Images/image18509.jpeg)

### FLOWS  FROM  IS  STANDARD

As discussed, a program will often need to obtain information  from a source or send information to a destination. For example, getting information  tion from, or send information to: a file on disk, the computer's memory  pain,  another program, Internet,  etc.

The communication between the origin of certain information and the destination is carried out  through  a  flow of  information (in  English  stream ).

![](Images/image18510.jpeg)

A stream is a data structure that acts as an intermediary between the program  ma and the origin or destination of the information. That is, the program will read or write  will go into the flow without caring where the information comes from or where it goes and  neither does it matter what type of data is read or written. This level of abstraction  tion  make  what  the  Program  no  have  what  to know  nothing  neither  the  device  neither  the  type  of information (simply read bytes or write bytes), which translates into a  ease  plus  to  hour  from  write programs.

So, for a program to get information from a source  you have to open a stream and analogously so that you can send information to a  destination. In the case of C/C++, when a program is executed, they are opened automatically.  automatically two streams: stdin ( standard input ), is the stream from the source, and  stdout  ( standard  output ),  is he  flow  to him  destination.

In C, stdin is bound to the keyboard and stdout to the screen. This this-  both the data that a program reads from stdin comes from the keyboard and all the data  who writes in  stdout are displayed  on  the screen.

### CHARACTER  FINISH  FROM  FILE

From the point of view of an application developer, an en-  trada or standard output is handled by the C language as if from a file  from  data  on  the  disk se  will try  A  file  from  data  no  it's more  what  a  collection  from

information. The data that we enter on the keyboard is a collection of  training and the data that we visualize on the monitor are also a collection  from  information.

![](Images/image18531.jpeg)![](Images/image18532.jpeg)![](Images/image18533.jpeg)![](Images/image18534.jpeg)end of  file

![](Images/image18535.jpeg)![](Images/image18536.jpeg)Beginning  the  file

Every file has a beginning and an end. How does a program know that it is  Reading  data  from  a  file,  what  I know  ha  arrived  to the  final  the  same  and,  by  it  so much,  no  is there more data? By an end-of-file mark. In the case of a recorded file  on a disc that mark will be written at the end of it. In the case of the keyboard  information comes from what we type, so if our program  ma requires to detect the end-of-file mark, we will have to type it when  Let's finish entering information. This is done by pressing the  keys  Ctrl+D  on  UNIX  or  Ctrl+Z  on  a  application  from  console  on  Windows.

Since a file or a device is always handled through a stream,  Talking about the end of the stream is synonymous with talking about the end of the file. Therefore, of  from now on, whenever we have to perform some kind of operation on  on a device or on a file, we will refer indistinctly to them or to the  flow  that represents them.

Remember that when the scanf function attempts to read an end-of-file character,  returns the EOF constant defined in the stdio.h file . The following example is-  write the message “End of data entry”, if the message “Price: ” responds-  We press the keys corresponding to the end of file character followed by the  Enter key ;  on  other  case,  will be written  the  price  keyed.

/*  eof.c

*/

#include  <stdio.h>

main()

{

int  r  =  0;

float  price  =  0;

printf("Price:  ");

r  =  scanf("%g",  &price);

(r  ==  EOF)  ?  printf("End  from  the  entry  from  data\n")

But this is not always so; Surely at some point we have had the need  ability to execute some sentences or others based on specific criteria.  two for us. On  a  case  What  East,  arises  the need for the program itself to make the decision, depending on the  value of the discriminant, whether what you have to calculate are two real roots or two  estate  complex conjugates.

Likewise, on more than one occasion we will need to execute a set of  tenences a certain number of times, or until a condition is met.  tion imposed by us. But if what we want is to read, not a  character but all that we write on the keyboard until we detect the end mark  from  file,  we will have  what to use  a  repetitive sentence.

In this chapter, you will learn how to write code for a program to make decisions.  sions  and  for  what  be  capable  from  run  blocks  from  sentences  repeated  times.

### JUDGMENT  if

The  judgment  if  It allows  to  a  Program  drink  a  decision  for  run  a  action  or another, based on the true or false result of an expression. syntax  for  use  this sentence  is the next:

judgment  1 ;  [else

judgment  2 ];

where condition is a numeric, relational, or logical expression and statement 1 and  statement 2 represent a simple or compound statement. Each sentence sim-  please  must end with  a  point  and  eat.

A  judgment  if  it  run  from  the  shape  following:

1. I know  evaluates  the  condition .

2. If the result of the evaluation of the condition is true (result different from  to  of 0),  will be executed  the indicated  by  sentence 1 .

3. Yes  the  result  from  the  evaluation  from  the  condition  is  fake  (result  0),  I know  axis-  cutar  it  indicated  by  the  judgment  2 ,  Yes  the  clause  else  I know  ha  specified.

4. Yes  the  result  from  the  evaluation  from  the  condition  is  fake,  and  the  clause  else  I know  ha  omitted, the  sentence 1  it is ignored.

5. On  any  case,  the  execution  keep going  on  the  following  judgment  executable.

Here are some examples for you to see in a simple way:  cilla  how is it used  sentence  if  .

### loops  nested

When a while statement is included  inside  another  while statement  , in general  a  while  ,  do  or  for statement  inside another one of them, we are in the case of loops  nested.  For example:

#include  <stdio.h>  main()

{

int  i  = 1,  j  =  1;

while  (  i  <=  3  ) //  While  i  be  less  or  same  what  3

{

printf("For  i  =  %d:  ",  i);

while  (  j  <=  4  )  //  While  j  be  less  or  same  what  4

{

printf("j  =  %d,  ",  j);

j++; //  increase  j  on  a  Unit

}

printf("\n"); //  advance  to  a  new  line  i++; //  increase  i  on  a  Unit

j  =  1; //  initialize  j  from  new  to  1

}

}

To the  run  East  Program  I know  gets  the  following  result:

| For | i | = | 1: | j | = | 1, | j | = | two, | j | = | 3, | j | = | 4, |
| For | i | = | two: | j | = | 1, | j | = | two, | j | = | 3, | j | = | 4, |
| For | i | = | 3: | j | = | 1, | j | = | two, | j | = | 3, | j | = | 4, |

The described process is repeated until the difference in absolute value of the  two last calculated approximations is as small as we want  (taking into account the limits established by the type of data used). According  this,  the  last  approach  be  a  root  valid,  when  I know  comply  what:

abs(r i  –  r i+1 )    

The  solution  from  East  trouble  can  be  from  the  following  shape:

double  approx; //  approach  to  the  root  square

*   When the condition specified in the  do ... while structure  shown above  is false, the process will be finished. It only remains to print the result  ted.

That when we type the second value, the first will be lost; when we type  the third, the second will be lost, and so on. ### INTRODUCTION  TO THE DIES

A matrix is a homogeneous structure, composed of several elements, all  of the same type and stored consecutively in memory. Each element  can be accessed directly by the name of the array variable followed by  one  or  more subscripts  locked between  brackets.

![](Images/image18561.jpeg)matrix  m

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

In general, the representation of the matrices is done by variables sub-  scripts or subscripts and can have one or more dimensions (subscripts). At  one-dimensional arrays are also called lists and two-dimensional arrays,  boards.

From a mathematical point of view, on more than one occasion we will need  use  subscripted variables such as:

v     to 0  ,  to 1  ,  to 2  ,...,  to i  ,...,  to n  

if two subscripts are used. This same representation can be used from a  programming language using the arrays we just defined and  what  then it  they study.

For example, suppose we have a one-dimensional array of integers  called m , which contains 10 elements. These items will be identified  following  shape:

![](Images/image18563.jpeg)matrix  m

|  |  |  | m[0] | m[1] | m[2] | m[3] | m[4] | m[5] | m[6] | m[7] | m[8] | m[9] |  |

Note that the subscripts are consecutive integers and that the first subscript  EC  okay  0.  A  subscript  can  be  any  expression  whole  positive.

Likewise, a two-dimensional matrix is represented by a varia-  ble with two subscripts (rows, columns); a three-dimensional matrix is represented  sits  through  a  variable  with  three  subscripts,  etc.  The  number  maximum  from  dimensions or the maximum number of elements, within the limits established  by  the  compiler,  for  a  matrix  depends  from  the  memory  available.

### ARRAYS  NUMERICAL  UNIDIMENSIONAL

As with other variables, before using an array you have to define  the. The definition of an array specifies the name of the array, the number of  elements  of the  same and  the  kind of these.

### Define  An array

The  definition  from  a  matrix  from  a  dimension  I know  make  from  the  shape  following:

type  name [ size ];

where type indicates the type of the elements of the array, which can be of any  any primitive or user-defined type; name is an identifier  names the array and size is an integer constant that specifies the number of  array elements. The square brackets modify the normal definition of the identifier.  cador  for  what  be  interpreted  by  the  compiler  What  a  matrix.

Let's look at some examples. The following lines of code are examples of  matrix definitions:

int  m[10];

float temperature[31];  structure  computer  steel[25];

Functions  gets  and  fgets

Other  shape  from  read  a  chain  from  characters  from  stdin  is  using  the  function  gets  ,  whose  syntax is as follows:

### To work  with  chains  from  characters

On  the  following  example  I know  treats  from  to write  a  Program  what  read  a  line  from  the  on-  standard trada and store it in a character array. Then use-  Using a function, we want to convert characters written in lowercase to  capital letters.

If you look at the ASCII table in the appendices of this book, you will see that the  characters 'A' , ..., 'Z' , 'a' , ... , 'z' are consecutive and in ascending order of their  code (values 65 to 122). So, passing a character from lowercase to uppercase  involves subtracting from the integer value (ASCII code) associated with the character the difference  difference between the codes of that character in lowercase and the same in uppercase.  For example, the difference 'a'–'A' is 97 – 32 = 65 , and is the same as 'b'–'B' , which  'c'–'C' , etc As an aid related to the above, you can review the concepts  previously exposed in this same chapter in the Marriage section.  ces  associative .

The function that performs this operation will receive as a parameter the array of  characters that contains the text to convert. If the function is called LowercaseMa-  capital letters  and  the  matrix  chain ,  the  call  it will be like this:

LowercaseUppercase(string);

As can be seen in the code shown below, the function returns  will receive the string you want to convert to uppercase. You will then access the  first element of the array and will check if it is a lowercase, in which  case will change the ASCII value stored in that element to the ASCII value  correspondent  to  capital letter. This  is:

void  LowercaseUppercase(char  str[])

{

int  i  =  0,  after  =  'to'  -  'TO';

for  (i  =  0;  str[i]  !=  '\0';  ++i)

if  (str[i]  >=  'to'  &&  str[i]  <=  'z')  str[i]  =  str[i]  -  after;

}

Notice that when the function LowercaseUppercase is called , what in  actually being passed is the address of the array. Therefore, the called function and the  calling function work on the same array, so the changes made  two  by a  or  other are visible  for both.

### STRUCTURES

All the variables that we have used so far allow us to store a piece of data and  of a single type, except for arrays that store multiple data but also  all of the same type. The purpose of a structure is to group one or more variables.  usually of different types, under the same name to make it easier to  cyl  its handling.

### Create  a  structure

To create a structure, you must define a new data type and declare a variable.  variable of this type. The declaration of a struct type includes both the elements  that compose it as its types. Each element of a structure receives the  member name (or field if we are talking about records). The syntax is as follows-  following:

structure  structure_type

{

type member_1 ;  type  member_2 ;

//  ...

type  member_n ;

}[ list  from  variables ];

The  struct keyword  tells the compiler that a structure is being defined.  structure; struct_type is an identifier that names the newly defined type;  and  every  member  can  be  from  a  type  primitive  (  char  ,  int  ,  float  ,  etc.)  or  a  type  from-  derived:  matrix,  pointer,  Union,  structure  or  function.  By  example:

structure  tfile  /*  statement  the  type  from  structure  tfile  */

{

char name[40];  char  address[40];  long  phone;

};

The declaration of a member of a structure cannot contain qualifications.  storage class parameters such as  extern  ,  static  ,  auto ,  or  register  and cannot  from  be started.

};

A structure in C can only contain members that correspond to  variable definitions. Instead, C++ allows a structure to contain,  what's more,  members  that are  definitions of  functions.

### JOINTS

A union is a storage region shared by two or more members.  usually of different types. This allows you to manipulate different types of data.  using  a  same  zone  from  memory,  the  reserved  for  the  variable  union .

The declaration of a union has the same form as the declaration of a  structure, except that instead of the keyword  struct  the keyword  reserved  union  . Therefore, everything exposed for the structures is applicable to  unions, with the exception that the members of a union do not have each  each one their own storage space, but they all share a single space.  space equal in size to the longest member in bytes. The syntax for  ra  declaring a join is  So:

### FIELDS  FROM  BITS

A  member  from  a  structure  (no  from  a  Union)  can  be  as well  a  countryside  from  bits ,  understanding  by  countryside  from  bits  a  set  from  bits  adjacent  inside  from  a

Unit  addressable,  usually  a  int  .  The  syntax  for  to declare  a  countryside  from  bits  is the next:

type  [ identifier ]  :  size

The size specifies the number of bits corresponding to the field and must be  a nonnegative integer constant that must not exceed the physical size of the pa-  till machine; that is, the size of an  int  . The type has to be whole. unlike-  ANSI C reference, which restricts the types of bit fields to  int  , or  unsigned  int  ,  C++  It allows  what  a  countryside  from  bits  be  from  any  type  whole;  is  say,  char  ,  short  ,  int  ,  long  ,  with  sign  or  without  sign,  or  a  type  listed.  No  I know  allow  arrays  from  fields  from  bits,  pointers  to  fields  from  bits  or  functions  what  return  a bit field. The field identifier is optional; an unidentified field  do  serves as  filling.

The assignment of the bit fields depends on the hardware; that is, the cam-  pos bits are assigned from most significant to least significant or vice versa,  case of the example shown below, depending on the machine used. He does-  next  example clarifies  the above.

/***********************  fields  from  bits  ***********************/

/*  bit_fields.c

*/

structure  word //  word  from  32  bits:  0  to  31

{

unsigned  car_ascii : 7; // bits 0 to 6  unsigned parity_bit : 1; // bit 7  unsigned  operation               :  5;  //  bits  8  to  12

unsigned :18;  //  bits  13  to  30  from  filling  unsigned  bit_sign :  1;  //  bit 31

};

main()  //  function  principal

{

structure  word  cb  =  {  'C',  1,  0x1E,  0  };

printf("bit fields: %x\n\n", cb);  printf("bit  from  sign : %x\n", cb.bit_sign);  printf("operation               : %x\n", cb.operation);  printf("bit  from  parity  :  %x\n",  cb.bit_parity);

printf("character  %c :  %x\n",  cb.car_ascii,  cb.car_ascii);

}

Using a bit field to save space is naive and  can lead to a loss of execution time. A pointer is a variable that contains the memory address of a piece of data or  another variable that contains the data. This means that the pointer points to the  physical space where the data or variable is. A pointer can point to an object  of any type, such as a structure or a function. The dots-  ers can be used to reference and manipulate data structures, to refer to  to provide dynamically allocated memory blocks and to provide memory passing  arguments for  reference  on  the  calls to  functions.

Many functions in the C library have parameters that are pointers and  they return a pointer. As an example, recall the syntax of the function  scanf or  of the function  strcpy.

When working with pointers, errors are common due to using them without  have been assigned a valid address; that is, pointers that, because they are not initialized  two point to no one knows where, producing access to memory areas not  allowed. Therefore, the utmost care must be taken so that this does not occur.  rra,  starting  adequately  every  one  from  the  pointers  what  let's use

As an application of the above, we are going to carry out a function CopiarMatriz  that allows you to copy an array of any data type and any number of  dimensions in another (it will be a function analogous to memcpy). In the previous chapter Earlier , the function CopiarMatriz that we developed there had the drawbacks  that it was not autonomous, because it depended on the ROWS and COLS constants , and on  that the size of the array was fixed by those constants. These drawbacks  can now be easily overcome using pointers, as you will see at  continuation.  The  CopyMatrix function  will have  the  following  prototype:

dest parameter is a generic pointer that will store the address of the  data destination array and orig is also a generic pointer that will store  the address of the source array. The size in bytes of both arrays is proportional.  tioned  through the  parameter  n .

What does the CopyMatrix function have to do ? Simply copy n bytes  from origin to dest . Think of an array, without thinking about the type of data it contains.  ne, it's not  more than a block of bytes  in a row  on  memory. Thinking  So,  orig is the start address of the block of bytes to be copied and dest is the address  tion of the block where they want to be copied. The copy will be done byte by byte, which  guarantees data type independence (the size of any data type is  multiple of a byte). This requires, as explained earlier in this same  chapter in the section Importance of the type of the object to which it points , convert  destination  and  original  to  pointers  to  char. Carrying out a study analogous to the one carried out for arrays of numeric pointers,  We will say that an array of pointers to character strings is a single array.  mensional in which each element is of type char * or unsigned char *. By  example:

It then assigns the element p[0] the address of c and writes its  contents. Similarly, we could proceed with the rest of the elements of the  matrix. Likewise, if an element like p[0] can point to a character, it also  It can also point to a character string or one-dimensional array of characters.  teres; in this case, the pointed character will match the first element  from  chain. For example:

### ASSIGNMENT  DYNAMIC  FROM  MEMORY

C has basically two methods for storing information in the  memory. The first uses global and local variables. In the case of variables  globals, the space is set to be used throughout the execution of the  Program; and in the case of local variables, the assignment is done through the pi-  that of the system; in this case, the space is fixed temporarily, while the variance  ble  exists.  The  second  method  uses  functions  belonging  to  the  library  from  C, such as malloc and free. Naturally, these functions use the memory area  estuary  free  for  perform  the  assignments  from  memory  and  set her free  when  be  precise.

The  assignment  dynamic  from  memory  consists  on  to assign  the  amount  from  memo-  would be necessary to store an object during program execution, rather than  to do so at compile time. When memory is assigned  For an object of any type, a pointer to the memory block is returned.  assigned death. According to this, what the compiler has to do is assign a  fixed amount of memory to store the address of the dynamically allocated object  cally, instead of making an assignment for the object itself. This implies declaration  Get a pointer to a data type equal to the type of the object you want to assign  dynamically. For example, if we want to dynamically allocate memory for  an array of integers, the object pointed to will be the first integer which implies de-  clarify  a pointer to  a  whole;  this is:

int  *p;

The C library essentially provides a function to allocate  dynamically die, malloc, and another to free the allocated memory space  for  an object when it  already  not necessary,  free.

malloc

The malloc function allows you to allocate a memory block of nbytes bytes consequent  files in memory to store one or more objects of any type. This  function returns a generic pointer (void *) that references the allocated space.  His  syntax is like this:

Therefore, for compatibility, it is recommended to perform  always the explicit conversion to the type of the variable used to store the  result. If there is insufficient memory space, the malloc function returns a  null pointer (value NULL or 0) and if the nbytes argument is 0, allocates a block of  size  0 returning  a pointer  valid.

### DECLARATIONS  COMPLEX

We understand by complex declaration an identifier qualified by more than one  operator (array: [], pointer:    , or function: () ). Various combinations can be applied  tions with these operators on an identifier; however, the elements of  an array cannot be functions, and a function cannot return a result.  ted  an array or a  function.

To interpret these statements, one must know that the brackets and parentheses  thesis (operators to the right of the identifier) take precedence over asterisks.  cos (operators to the left of the identifier). Parentheses and brackets have  the same priority and are evaluated from left to right. As a last step,  applies the specified type. Using parentheses, we can change the order of  priorities.  The  expressions  Come in  parenthesis  I know  evaluate  First,  from  plus  internal  to  more external.

An easy way to interpret complex statements is to read them from  inside  toward  outside,  Following  the  Steps  indicated  to  continuation:

1. Begin  with  the  identifier  and  look  Yes  toward  the  right  there are  brackets  or  pa-  renthesis

2. Interpret  those  brackets  or  parenthesis  and  look  Yes  toward  the  left  the  identi-  maker  there are asterisks.

3. Within each level of parentheses, from innermost to outermost, apply the  rules 1  and  two.

2. An algorithm that generates a random or apparently random sequence of  numbers is called a random number generator. Many programs require  of an algorithm like this. The most commonly used algorithm to generate  random numbers is the one of linear congruence that is stated as follows-  tea:

rk _  =  (multiplier  *  rk -1  +  increase)  %  module

where it is observed that each number in the sequence r k  is calculated from your  predecessor r k-1  (% is the modulus or remainder operator of an integer division). the se-  sequence, thus generated, is more correctly called a pseudo-random sequence, since  what  every  number  generated  depends  the  previously  generated.

The  function  rand  from  the  library  of C  is  based  on  East  algorithm.

The following function uses the algorithm  linear congruence to generate  a random number between 0 and 1, and will not cause overshoot on a computer  what  admit a range  from  integers of  –2 31 to  2 31–1 .

double  rnd(long  *prandom)

{

In this way, the function will be able to modify the  argument  past  with  the  value  the  latest  number  pseudorandom  calculated,  it  which will allow to calculate the next pseudo-random number based on the previous one.  It can be seen that the calculated pseudo-random number is actually a variable.  lor between 0 and 65535 and that to convert it to a value between 0 and 1 we divide it by  65535;  the type quotient  double  is  the value returned by  the function.

The following program shows how to use the rnd function to generate numbers.  groupers  pseudo random between 0  and  1:

### PASS  A  POINTER  WHAT  ARGUMENT  TO  A  FUNCTION

A pointer, like other types of variables, can be passed by value or by  reference. By value means that the value stored (an address) in the parameter  current parameter (argument specified in the function call) is copied to the  corresponding formal parameter (parameter declared in the function header)  tion); if we now modify the value of this formal parameter, the current parameter  correspondent  no  I know  go  affected.  On  the  Program  previous,  when  main  invoke  to the Display function , the current parameter m is passed by value. This means  that the address stored in m is copied into the formal parameter x of Display ,  so that even if this function modified the address stored in x , m  would remain unchanged. By reference , what is copied is not the stored address.  stored in the current parameter, but rather the address at which that parameter is located.  current parameter, such that a reference to the content of the formal parameter is  a  parameter reference  current.

To clarify what has been said, we are going to modify the previous program in the following way:  that includes an AssignMem2D function and another LiberarMem2D that allow,  respectively, allocate memory for a two-dimensional array and free it.  Suppose that the approach we make for this program, strictly speaking,  burning,  is like this:

The function is executed  AssignMem2D and x takes a new value: the address  the  block  from  memory  reserved  by  malloc  .  Ha  changed  m  on  the  same  value?  Obviously not, since both x and m are local variables to their respective  functions and are not related to each other. Therefore, m follows va-  reading  NULL  , so the program doesn't work. Also, when the function  AssignMem2D completes, the local variable x will be destroyed and a block of  memory  without  reference  and  without  break free  (I know  ha  generated  a  lagoon  from  memory).

### DATA  RETURNED  BY  A  FUNCTION

A function can return any value of a primitive or derived type, ex-  I accept an array (not dynamic) or a function. When a function returns a value  lor, what it actually returns is a copy of that value, which is usually  stored in a variable of the same type. Therefore, it can return a  integer, a structure, a pointer, etc., but not an array because if these are  san by reference, they would also be returned by reference; this means that the  function would return its starting address and not a copy of its elements;  after the above, you may be thinking, if it returns the starting address  zo, couldn't we use it to access your data? Well no, because logically  Thus, the array we are trying to return will have been defined as a structure of  data local to it, and therefore will be destroyed when the function ends.  This same error will occur whenever we return the address of any  variable  local  with  the  intention  from  to access  plus  afternoon  to the  value  what  stored.

*   A  copy  from  the  data.
*   The  address  from  a  block  from  memory  reserved  dynamically  for  conte-  ner  the data.
*   The  address  from  a  variable  declared  static  .

### ARGUMENTS  ON  THE  LINE  FROM  ORDERS

Many times, when we invoke a program from the operating system, we need to  we need to write one or more arguments after the name of the program.  ma,  separated  by  a  space  on  White.  By  example,  think  on  the  order  ls  -l  the

UNIX operating system or in the dir /p command of the Windows console. both ls  as dir are programs; -l and /p are options or arguments on the command line  that we pass to the program so that it has a different behavior than it has  from  shape  default;  is  say,  when  no  I know  pass  arguments.

In the same way, we can build programs that support ar-  arguments via the command line. What function will receive those arguments?  Logically the  main function  , since it is through this function where it begins to  run a C program. Does this mean that the  main function  has to have  formal parameters where the passed arguments are stored, just as occurs  rre with any other function. Thus, the prototype of the  main function  in general is  from  the following way:

int  main(int  argc ,  char  * argv []);

The  argument  argc  is  a  whole  what  indicates  the  number  from  arguments  past  via the command line, including the name of the program. The argument  argv is an array of pointers to character strings. Every element of this  array points to one argument, so argv[0] contains the name of the  program, argv[1] the first command line argument, argv[2] the second  argument etc The  main function  returns an  int  with which we can express the  success  or not  from  the  execution  of happiness  function.

For example, suppose we have a C program called test that  accepts -n and -l as arguments . So we could call this application  writing  on  the  line  from  orders  the  system  operative  the  following  order:

test  -n  -l

This makes argc automatically take the value 3 (program name  plus two arguments) and that the first element of the pointer array points to the  program name and the following two, to each of the arguments. Can  imagine  this matrix  from the way  following:

### REDIRECTION  FROM  THE  ENTRY  AND  FROM  THE  EXIT

Redirecting the input means that the data can be obtained from a medium  different from standard input; for example, from a file on disk. If suppose- We see that we have a program called redir.c that accepts data from the input  standard, the following command would execute the redir program and get the data from  entry  from  a  file  on  the  disk  called  fdata.ent .

redeem  <  fdatos.ent

Likewise, redirecting the output means sending the results it produces  a program to a device other than standard output; for example, to a fi-  file on disk. Taking the redir.c program as an example , the following command  would execute  the  Program  redeem  and  I would write  the  results  on  a  file  fdata.out .

redeem  >  fdata.salt

Note that the program is run from the command line, which to redeem  redirect the input, use the “<” symbol and that to redirect the output,  use the “>”. It is also possible to redirect input and output simultaneously.  mind.  For example:

redeem  <  fdatos.ent  >  fdata.salt

As an application of the above, we are going to make a program that reads a  set of numbers and write them in one format or another, depending on the  arguments passed through the command line. That is, if the program is called  ma  redir.c ,  the  order  redeem  will visualize  the  set  from  numbers  without  plus,  but  the  or-

give  redeem  –l  will visualize  the  set  from  numbers  writing  to  continuation  from  AC-  gives  one  from  they  a  message  what  indicate  Yes  is  pair  or  odd.  By  example:

| 24 | is | pair |
| 3\. 4\. 5 | is | odd |
| 7... | is... | odd |

The  code  from  East  Program  I know  sample  to  continuation.

*/

#include  <stdio.h>

return  0;

}

### FUNCTIONS  RECURSIVE

A function is said to be recursive if it calls itself. The C compiler  allows any number of recursive calls to a function. Every time the  function is called, the formal parameters and the  auto  and  register variables  are  started. Note that  static  variables are only initialized once, in the  first  call.

When is it efficient to write a recursive function? The answer is simple:  when the process to be programmed is by definition recursive. For example, the calculation  the factorial of a number, n! = n(n–1)! , is by definition a recursive process  what  I know  states like this:  factorial(n)  = n  *  factorial(n–1) .

Therefore, the best way to program this problem is by implementing  a recursive function. As an example, here is a program that  visualize  the  factorial  from  a  number.  For  it,  I know  ha  written  a  function  factorial

what  receives  What  parameter  a  number  whole  positive  and  bring back  What  result  the  factorial of that number.

/*************  Calculation  the  factorial  from  a  number  *************/

/*  factorial.c

*/

#include  <stdio.h>

unsigned  long  factorial(int  n);  main()

{

int number;  unsigned  long  fact;

do

{

printf("Number?  ");  scanf("%d",  &number);

}

while  (number  <  0  ||  number  >  25);  fact  =  factorial(number);

printf("\nThe  factorial  from  %d  is  %ld\n",  number,  fact);

}

| Level  from  recursion | Process  from  Going  (battery  from  calls) | Process  from  lap |
| 0 | factorial(4) | 24 |
| 1 | 4  *  factorial(3) | 4*6 |
| two | 3  *  factorial(2) | 3*2 |
| 3 | two  *  factorial(1) | twenty-one |
| 4 | 1  *  factorial(0) | eleven |

Each call to the factorial function increases the recurrence level by one unit.  Zion. When n = 0 is reached , the value 1 is obtained as a result and the  return to the starting point, reducing the recursion level by one unit  every time. The center

![](Images/image18693.jpeg)![](Images/image18694.jpeg)![](Images/image18695.jpeg)![](Images/image18696.jpeg)![](Images/image18697.jpeg)each of the pending calls. Graphically we can represent this process  cease  So:

| main{ | 4 | factorial(4){ | 3 | factorial(3){ | two | factorial(2){ | 1 | factorial(1){ | 0 | factorial(0){ |
| factorial(4) |  | n  =  4 |  | n  =  3 |  | n  =  two |  | n  =  1 |  | n  =  0 |
| } | 24 | 4*factorial(3)} | 6 | 3*factorial(2)} | two | 2*factorial(1)} | 1 | 1*factorial(0)} | 1 | 1} |

![](Images/image18698.jpeg)![](Images/image18699.jpeg)![](Images/image18700.jpeg)![](Images/image18701.jpeg)![](Images/image18702.jpeg)Note that the factorial run starts five times; when you re-  solve factorial(0) there are still four calls to solve; when  resolve factorial(1) there are still three calls pending to resolve; etc. Observe-  var also that the parameter n is a local variable to the function, so it is pre-  feel  with  its value  local  in each  a  of the  executions.

Conclusion, for each recursive execution of the function, a certain quantity is needed.  memory to store local variables and the current state of the  calculation process in order to recover said data when an execution is finished.  cution and have to resume the previous one. For this reason, in practical applications  it is imperative to show that the maximum level of recursion is not only finite, but  Really  small.

As stated above, recursive algorithms are particularly appropriate  when the problem to be solved or the data to be treated are defined recursively.  However, the use of recursion should be avoided when there is an obvious solution  by  iteration.

### POINTERS  TO  FUNCTIONS

As with arrays, the name of a function represents the address  tion where that function is located; this means that as such an address, it can  passed as an argument to a function, store it in a pointer (which can be  be an element of an array), etc. The syntax for declaring a pointer to a  function  is like this:

type  (* p_identif )();

where type is the type of the function return value and p_identif is the name of  a  variable  from  type  pointer.  This  variable  will store  the  address  from  Start  from  a  function,  Dadaist  by  the  own self  Name  from  the  function.  By  example:

double  (*pfn)();

indicates that pfn is a pointer to a function that returns a value of type  double  .  Notice the parentheses around the identifier in the declaration; they are fun-  damentals.  Yes  no  the  we put,  the  meaning  change  completely.  Let's see:

double  *pfn();

indicates  what  nfp  is  a  function  what  bring back  a  pointer  to  a  value  from  type  double  .

Continuing with the pfn declaration , we know that the function pointed to has  to return a value of type  double  , but what arguments does it have? The answer  is: any number and type of arguments because in C the absence of arguments  indicates that, any number and type of arguments, instead if between the parent-  if we write  void  , it means no arguments (in C++, both forms, parentheses  empty  or  parenthesis  with  void  ,  mean  it  same:  function  without  arguments).

As an example, suppose that in a program we have two functions defined:  tions  whose prototypes are  So:

double square(double);  double  pot(double,  double);

As stated, any of these functions can be assigned to pfn co-  mo  shown below:

nfp  =  square;  nfp  =  pot;

Finally, to call the function pointed to by pfn , you can use any  want  in the following two ways:

(*pfn)( arguments );  pfn( arguments );

As explained,  pfn , as defined, we can use  with  different  functions  regardless  from  his  number  and  type  from  parameters.  What is not possible is to use this pointer to call a function with a  type of the result different from the one specified when declaring said pointer. For example,  Yes  declared the pot function like this:

int  pot(int,  int);

the assignment pfn = pot would result in an error because the pointer represents a  function  what  bring back  a  double  and  pot  is  a  function  what  bring back  an  int  .

Similarly,  as well  can  define  a  pointer  for  a  type  specific  of functions. For example, for functions with an argument of type  double  and that  return  a  value  from  type  double  ,  the  statement  would  So:

double  (*pfn)(double);

In this case, the assignment to  pfn of the square function would be correct, but  no  it  would  the  assignment  from  the  function  pot  because  have  two  arguments.

### OVERVIEW OF I/O FLOWS

Communication between the program and the source or destination of certain information  It is done through a flow of information (in English stream ) that is nothing more than  a data structure that acts as an intermediary between the program and the source or  the destination of the information. That is, the program will read or write to the stream without  care where the information comes from or where it goes and neither does it care  type of the data being read or written. This level of abstraction makes the pro-  grama  no  have  what  to know  nothing  neither  the  device  neither  the  type  from  information,  it  what  I know  translate  on  a  ease  plus  to  the  hour  from  to write  programs.

### I/O USING REGISTERS

Data can be written and read in blocks called registers with the  fwrite  and  fread  functions ; that is, as a fixed-length data set, so  them as structures or elements of an array. However, although the most common  Whether a record corresponds to a data structure, it is feasible  also that a record corresponds to a variable of type  char  ,  int  ,  float  or  with a string of characters, among others, which means that these functions  they can  replace  to  the  functions  standard  from  IS  studied  until  now.

### fwrite

This function allows you to write a block of bytes seen byte by byte; that is, without you-  ner  on  bill  the  type  from  the  data  what  is it so  stored  on  the  same.

#include  <stdio.h>

size_t  fwrite(const  void  * buffer ,  size_t  no ,  size_t  c ,  FILE  * ff );

Compatibility :  ANSI,  UNIX  and  Windows

According to the presented prototype, the function  fwrite  allows to write c  elements of length n bytes ( c × n bytes) stored in the specified buffer ,  in the file associated with pf . Returns the number of elements currently is-  crits. If this number is less than c , then an error has occurred. See-  mos  An example:

FILE  *pf1  =  NULL,  *pf2  =  NULL;

char  car,  string[36];

pf1  =  fopen("f1.txt",  "wb");

pf2  =  fopen("f2.txt",  "wb");

fgets(string,  36,  stdin);  car  =  getchar();

//  ...

fwrite(&car, sizeof(char), 1, pf1);  fwrite(string,  strlen(string),  1,  pf2);

The last two sentences are equivalent to the following:  tion:

fputc(char, pf1);  fputs(string,  pf2);

The  fwrite function  stores numeric data in binary format. This  means that an  int  occupies four bytes, a  long  occupies four bytes, a  float  occupies  four  bytes,  a  double  occupies  eight  bytes,  etc.

■ On Windows, don't confuse the binary format used to store  a numerical data, with the binary form ( b ) in which a file can be opened for  prevent it from happening  the translation  of the character  '\n'  to  CR+LF and  vice versa.

### fred

This  function  It allows  read  a  block  from  bytes,  byte  to  byte;  the  type  from  the  data  to  what  give  place  it will depend  of the  variable  what  store them.

#include  <stdio.h>

size_t  fread(void  * buffer ,  size_t  no ,  size_t  c ,  FILE  * ff );

Compatibility :  ANSI,  UNIX  and  Windows

According to the presented prototype, the  fread function  allows to read c ele-  elements of length n bytes ( c × n bytes) of the file associated with pf and the stores  na  on  the  buffer  specified.  Bring back  the  number  from  elements  at the moment  read; if this value is less than c , either an error occurred or the end was reached  of the file. To distinguish if the end of the file has been detected or if it has occurred  an error, we will have to use the functions  feof  or  ferror  . If n or c are 0,  fread  bring back  a  0  and  the  contents  the  buffer  it remains  same.  Let's see  a  example:

FILE  *pf1  =  NULL,  *pf2  =  NULL;

char  car,  string[36];

pf1  =  fopen("f1.txt",  "rb");

pf2  =  fopen("f2.txt",  "rb");

//  ...

fread(&car, sizeof(char), 1, pf1);  fread(string,  sizeof(string)-1,  1,  pf2);

The last two sentences are equivalent to the following:  tion  (on  the  example,  fred  will read  until  sizeof(string)-1  characters  or  until  the  finish  the  file,  like  fgets  ):

car  =  fgetc(pf1);

fgets(string,  sizeof(string),  pf2);

The examples given in the  fwrite  and  fread sections  show that  these functions allow writing and reading, respectively, variables of type  char  ,  int  ,  float  , arrays, structures (we will see this next), etc. This is,  they can  replace  perfectly  to  fputc  and  fgetc  ,  to  puts  and  fgets  ,  etc.

### OPENING  FILES  FOR  ACCESS  SEQUENTIAL

The simplest type of access to a data file is sequential: records  that are written to the file are automatically placed one after  from another, and when you read them, you start with the first, continue with the next,  and so on until the end is reached. This way of proceeding enables  the  records  can  be  from  any  length,  even  from  a  only  byte.

This type of access is generally used with text files in which  writes all the information from the beginning to the end and reads the same  shape. On the other hand, text files are not the most appropriate for storing  large series of numbers, because each number is stored as a sequence  cia of bytes; this means that a nine-digit integer occupies nine  bytes instead of the four required for an integer. Hence, for the treat-  I lie  from  information  numerical  I know  suggest  use  fwrite  and  fred  .

### A  example  from  access  sequential

After the theory presented so far about working with files, there will be  observed that the work methodology is repeated. That is, to write data to  a  file:

*   We define  a  flow  toward  the  file  on  the  what  we wish  to write  data.

*   We read the data from the input device or from another file, perform the  operations that are precise and we write them in our file. The data  usually  they will be  writings  record  to  record  using  the  fwrite  function .
*   AND  Finally,  we close  the  flow.

AND  for  read  data  from  a  file  existing:

*   We open  a  flow  from  the  file  the  which  we want  read  the  data.
*   We read the data from the file and store it in variables of our program.  grass in order to work with them. The data will normally be read re-  record  to record  using the  function  fred  .
*   AND  Finally,  we close  the  flow.

This shows that a file is nothing more than a permanent medium  data storage, which makes that data available to any pro-  grass that needs handling. Logically, the data must be recovered  of the file with the same format with which they were written, otherwise the  results  they will be  unexpected. By  example, if  in the next exercise  the data  are stored in the order: a string, another string and a  long  , must be retrieved  in that order and with that same format. It would be a mistake to first retrieve a  long  , then a string and finally the other string, or retrieve a string first  chain,  then  a  float  and  Finally  the  other  chain;  etc.

### CONTROL  THE  BUFFER  ASSOCIATED  WITH  A  FLOW

As we have seen, the functions used to perform I/O operations they use a buffer in order to make them more efficient. A buffer is nothing more than  a data area in system memory (RAM memory) allocated by the program.  gram when creating a stream associated with a file. What is the purpose of this  buffer ? If a stream did not have an associated buffer , each byte written to or read from  from,  the  file  would  physically  transferred  on  the  moment  from  the  operation.  On

contrast, when a stream has a buffer associated with it , all I/O operations re-  wanted are served from that buffer , and the physical transfer of data is done in  multiples  of the size of  buffer .

By default, when a program creates a stream, it allocates a one-size buffer to it.  specific size (for example, 4,096 bytes). However, the C library  provides functions that allow you to control whether or not a buffer exists , like so  What  his  size; by  example  setvbuf  .

### setvbuf

This function allows the user to control the existence or not of a buffer and the size  hand of the same The  setvbuf function  must be executed after the file is opened and  before any read or write operation, or after having called  mado  to  the  function  fflush  .  The  prototype  from  is  function  is  So:

#include  <stdio.h>

int  setvbuf(FILE  * pf ,  char  * buffer ,  int  mode ,  size_t  n );  Compatibility :  ANSI,  UNIX  and  Windows

buffer argument is a character array of length n bytes that defines  performs the function of buffer or intermediate memory; the mode argument can  be: _IOFBF or _IONBF. The first allows allocating a buffer of n bytes and the second  second  indicates that  will not be used  a buffer.

The  setvbuf function  returns 0 on success and a value  different  from 0 in case  contrary.

The following program counts the lines of a text file. The account the  makes  three times:

*   using  a  buffer  from  size  BUFSIZ  bytes.
*   using  a  buffer  from  size  2,048  bytes.
*   Without  use  a  buffe r.

The program returns the time, expressed in seconds, that it takes  to count the number of lines in the file passed as an argument to  the  command line.

The  Program  full  I know  sample  to  continuation.

pf  =  open(argv[1]);

### fflush

The  fflush function  writes to the file associated with the stream pointed to by pf the  content of the buffer defined for this stream. On Windows, not UNIX, if the fi-  le instead of being open for writing is open for reading,  fflush  deletes the  contents  the  buffer .

#include <stdio.h>  int  fflush(FILE  * ff );

Compatibility :  ANSI,  UNIX  and  Windows

The  fflush function  returns the value 0 if it executes successfully, if the flux does not have  ne  a  buffer  or  Yes  was  opened  for  read  only;  on  other  case,  bring back  a  EOF  .

### OPENING  FILES  FOR  ACCESS  RANDOM

Up to this point, we have worked with files according to the following scheme:  burn: open the file, read or write to the end of it, and close the file.  But we have not read or written from a certain position within the fi-  chero. This is particularly important when we need to modify some  of the values contained in the file or when we need to extract a part  concrete  inside the file.

A randomly accessed file is comparable to an array. In a ma-  triz to access one of its elements we use an index. In a file accessed  said  randomly  the  index  is  substituted  by  a  pointer  from  YOU.  Saying  pointer  is automatically placed at the beginning of the file when the file is opened for reading  and/or write, and can also be moved to any other position in the file  calling the  fseek function  discussed earlier in this chapter. Re-  remember that a read or write operation begins at the position where  where the R/W pointer is and that when that operation completes, its position will match  with  the  byte  just  next  the  latest  read or  written.

At the beginning of this section we said that random access to files is par-  Particularly important when we need to modify some of the values  contained in the file, or when we need to extract a specific part  inside the file. This can be quite tricky if the units of  recording that we have called records are not all the same, since they intervene  nen the factors of: position where a record begins and length of the record.  Note that when you need to replace the nth record of a file with  other, it must not exceed the number of bytes it currently has. All of this is  feasible by counting in a matrix the starting position of each of the  records and each of the fields if necessary (this information is stored  would dine in an index file for later use), but it is much more  easy  Yes  everyone  the registers  have  the same  length.

As an example, we are going to write a program fseek.c that allows us to modify the  phone list created with the fwrite.c program made earlier. East  new program opens a file containing records of type  record (created  by the program fwrite.c ), computes its number of records, requests the number of  record to be modified, displays it on the screen and asks if you want to modify it.  ditify; if so, it requests from the keyboard the new data for that record and  stores it in the same position within the file by rewriting the first record  mitive. Next, it asks again for the number of the next register to  Modify;  a value  0, end  the program.

For  calculate  number  from  records  from  a  file  we will proceed  So:

fseek(pf,  0L,  SEEK_END);

totalreg  =  ftell(pf)/sizeof(record);

First  we situate  the  pointer  from  YOU  to the  final  the  file  for  can  calculate  with  ftell  the  length  the  same  and  then  we divide  the  length  the  file  Come in  the  length of a record.

For  Modify  a  record  it  habitual  is:

The C preprocessor is a word processor that manipulates the text of a file.  source le as part of the first phase of translating the source code of a  C program and before the compilation itself begins. The part  from  text  manipulated  I know  known  What  guidelines  for  the  preprocessor .

A directive is an instruction to the C preprocessor. Directives  tell the preprocessor what specific actions to perform and generalize  mind are used to make programs easy to modify and compile into  different execution environments. For example, replace elements in the text,  insert the contents of other files into the source file or suppress compilation  tion  of parts of  file  source.

The  preprocessor  from  C  recognize  the  following  guidelines:

| #define | #endif | #ifdef | #line |
| #elif | #error | #ifndef | #pragma |
| #else | #if | #include | #undef |

The # symbol must be the first character, other than whitespace, in the  line containing the leader; between the # symbol and the first letter of the address  thrice white space characters may appear. A guideline that occupies more than  a  line  physical  can  be  continued  on  a  line  following,  placing  the  character

\  immediately  before  from  change  to  the  line  following.  By  example:

#define T_INITIAL(description) \  printf("\n\nfor  :  %s",  #description);\  initial  =  clock();

Any text that follows a directive, except an argument or a value that  shape  part  from  the  directive,  have  what  be  included  What  a  comment  (/     /).

#define  T_INITIAL(description)  /*  description  is  a  parameter  */  \  printf("\n\nfor  :  %s",  #description);\

initial  =  clock();

A directive can be written anywhere in the source file, but only  the mind  I know  apply  from  his  point  from  definition  until  the  final  from  saying  file.

### DIRECTIVE  #define

The #define directive is used to associate identifiers with keywords,  constants,  sentences  and  expressions.  When  a  identifier  It represents  a  constant is called a symbolic constant ; Instead, when an identifier  represents statements or expressions is called a macro . The syntax for this di-  rectrix  can  be  from  two  shapes:  without  parameters  and  with  parameters:

#define  identifier  text

#define  identified r( parameters )  text

The #define directive replaces all occurrences of identifier or identifier .  cador ( parameters ) in the source file by text . Parameter s represents a list  of formal parameters enclosed in parentheses and separated by commas, which in the substitution  tion, they will be replaced by their corresponding current parameters, called  also arguments. Between the identifier and the open parenthesis there cannot be  a  space  on  White,  for  no  confuse  the  parameters  with  the  text .

For clarity of the program, the symbolic constants usually express-  I know  on  capital letters  with  the  finish  from  distinguish them  from  the  others  variables.

#define  WIDTH  70

#define  LENGTH  (WIDTH  +  10)

These directives define a symbolic constant WIDTH of value 70 and another  value LENGTH WIDTH + 10 ; that is, 70+10 . Every appearance of  WIDTH  in the source file is replaced by 70 and each occurrence of LENGTH , by  ( 70+10 ). The parentheses in many cases are necessary to obtain the results.  two expected; in any case, they make the definition of the  constant  or  from  the  macro.  By  example,  suppose  the  following  judgment:

var  =  LENGTH  *  fifteen;

Then  from  the  substitution  would:

var  =  (70  +  10)  *  fifteen;

In the case of not having used parentheses in the definition of LENGTH , the  result would be:

what  would give  place  to  a  result  different.

The  following  line  from  code  is  a  example  from  a  macro  with  two  parameters:

#define  MINOR(a,  b)  ((to)  <  (b)  ?  (to)  :  (b))

This guideline defines the macro named LESS , in order to get the  smallest value among the current parameters, when substitution is performed. By  example,  a  idea  at  Program  source like:

### macro  predefined

ANSI C recognizes five predefined macros. The name of each of them  preceded and followed by two underscores. These macros are (see also  a  little later the  directive  line):

Macro Description

_ _DATE_ _  This macro is replaced by a string of characters of the form  ma  hmm  dd  aaaa  (Name  the  month,  day  and year). By  example:

_ _TIME_ _  This macro is replaced by a string of characters of the form  ma  hh:mm:ss  (hour,  minutes  and  seconds).  By  example:

_  _FILE_  _ This  macro  is  replaced by  the  Name  the  file  source  current.

By  example:

_ _LINE_ _  This macro is replaced by the integer corresponding to the number  from  current line.  For example:

_ _STDC_ _ This macro is replaced with the value 1 if the option  /Za or    std1  has been specified. This option verifies that all code is-  tea  according  to  the  ANSI standards  c.  By  example:

int  ANSI  =  STDC  ;

### The  operator  #

The # operator is only used with macros that have parameters. When  this operator precedes the name of a formal parameter in the definition of the  macro, the corresponding current parameter will be enclosed in double quotes and  treaty  as a literal.  For example:

#define  LITERAL(s)  printf(#s  "\n")

A  idea  What:

LITERAL(Press  a  key  for  continue);

would  replaced  by:

printf("Press  a  key  for  continue"  "\n");  equivalent  to:  printf("Press  a  key  for  continue\n");

### The  operator  ##

The ## operator is used only with macros that have parameters. It allows  the  concatenation  fingers  chains. By  example:

#define  OUTPUT(n)  printf("element  "  #n  "  =  %d\n",  element##n)

A  idea  What:

OUTPUT(1);

would  replaced  by:

printf("element  "  "1"  "  =  %d\n",  element1);  equivalent  to:  printf("element  1  =  %d\n",  element1);

### DIRECTIVE  #error

### UTILIZATION  FROM  FILES  FROM  HEADBOARD

The #include directive adds the contents of a text file to a program.  source. Therefore, it is useful to write the definitions of constants, macros, declarations,  variable rations, user-defined data types, function prototypes,  tions,  etc.,  what  possibly  they will be  used  on  different  programs,  on  files  what  then  we will include  by  means, medium  from  the  directive  #include.  By  example:

************************************************** **************/

*

*  The  two  lines  following  include  the  files  specified

*/

{

char  message[25];  RegType  record;

log = ReadLog();  Verify(record,  message);  putchar('\n');

puts(message);

}

This program calls the  functions  ReadLog and Verify . Therefore,  it is necessary to previously specify the prototypes of these functions. This is  justly  it  what  I know  makes the  include  the  file  declare1.h .

/***************************************************** ***************

DECLARATIONS

************************************************** **************/

/*  declare1.h

*/

#if  !defined(_DECLARA1_H)  #define  _DECLAR1_H

RegType  ReadRecord(void);

void  Check(RegType  record,  char  *message);  #endif  // _DECLARA1_H

Note that the prototypes of the functions mentioned above for  they will become part of the program code only if they have not already been included.  This  is the  purpose of the  guidelines:

#if  !defined(_DECLARA1_H)  #define  _DECLAR1_H

//  ...  #endif

Note that the preprocessor will only include the code between #define and  #endif if the constant _DECLARA1_H is not defined; in this case, define that  constant, and the prototypes of the functions and other declarations, when they exist.  so, they will become part of the program. If during this phase of the processing  duction of the source file there would be a second attempt to include the contents of the  file declare1.h , it will fail because the constant _DECLARA1_H is already declared.  finished. This way of proceeding is nothing more than a security measure to avoid  during the compile phase (not during the bind phase) that the declarations  contained in a file can be included twice in the same module or  translation unit, which would lead to redefinition errors. This case could  occur, for example, when two or more files included in a module include  his  once a same  file.

As well,  I know  can  observe  what  the  prototypes  from  the  functions  ReadLog  and Check use the RegType user-defined type . Therefore, it is necessary It is advisable to include the declaration of the TipoReg type before the prototypes of the  functions. DECLARATIONS

*/

{

}  RegType;

#endif  //  _DECLARA2_H

Introduce  a  character:  TO  01000001

Character  reflected:  and  10000010

The  structure  the  Program  will consist  from  the  functions  following:

a) A main main function that will call a ReflectByte macro that inverts  ta the order of the bits (bit 0 will become bit 7, bit 1 will become bit 6,  the  bit  two  it will happen  to  be  the  bit  5,  etc.)  and  to  a  function  Visualize  for  show  the

introduced character and the one reflected in the previously exposed form (symbols  licly  on  hexadecimal  and in binary).

b) A  macro  ReflectByte e:

#define  ReflectByte(  b  )

This  macro  will receive  What  parameter  a  byte  b  and  give to  What  result  the  byte  reflected.

c) A  function  Visualize  with  the  prototype  following:

void  Visualize(  unsigned  char  c  );

This  function  will receive  What  parameter  the  character  what  I know  wants  visualize  and  it  will present  symbolically, in hexadecimal  and  in binary.

The  Program  full  I know  sample  to  continuation.

/*****************  Reflect  a  byte  *****************/

/*  refect.c

*/

#include  <stdio.h>

#define  ReflectByte(  c  )\

((((c)&0x01)  <<  7)  |  (((c)&0x02)  <<  5)  |\

(((c)&0x04)  <<  3)  |  (((c)&0x08)  <<  1)  |\

(((c)&0x10)  >>  1)  |  (((c)&0x20)  >>  3)  |\

(((c)&0x40)  >>  5)  |  (((c)&0x80)  >>  7))

void  Visualize(  unsigned  char  c  );  main()

{

printf("Enter  a  character:  ");  c  =  getchar();

display(c);

c  =  ReflectByte(c);

printf("\nCharacter  reflected:  %c\n",  c);  display(c);

}

{

for  (i  =  7;  i>=0;  i--)

{

printf("\ni  =  %d  ",  i);

printf("%d",  (c  &  (1  <<  i))  ?  1  :  0);

}

printf("\n");

}

The main characteristic of dynamic structures is the power they have  to vary its size and there are many problems that require this type of structure.  structures. This property clearly distinguishes them from functional static structures.  damentals  What  the  arrays.  When  I know  creates  a  matrix  his  number  from  elements  is fixed at that instant and then cannot be enlarged or reduced element by  element, conserving the currently allocated space; instead, when  creates  a  dynamic structure  Yes indeed  it's possible.

Therefore, it is not possible to allocate a fixed amount of memory for a structure.  dynamic structure, and as a consequence a compiler cannot associate addresses  explicit with the elements of such structures. The technique most frequently used  frequently to solve this problem consists of making a direct assignment  dynamics for the individual elements, as they are created during the  execution of the program, rather than making the assignment all at once for a  number  Of elements  determined.

When working with dynamic structures, the compiler allocates a quantity  fixed amount of memory to maintain dynamically assigned element address  mind, instead of making an assignment for the element itself. This implies that  there should be a clear distinction between data and references to data, and that consequently  data types whose values are references to other data must be used.  cough;  us  we're  referring  to  the  variables  of type  "pointer  to".

When  I know  assign  memory  dynamically  for  a  object  from  a  type  any-  ra, a pointer to the allocated memory area is returned. To perform this operation  ration we have in C the function  malloc  (see in chapter 7, the section  Assignment  memory dynamics ).

This chapter introduces various algorithms for building abstract structures  of data. After you have worked through the examples in this chapter, you will be able to  exploit the power of linked lists, stacks, queues, and trees in your applications.  them  binaries.

### LINEAR LISTS

So far we have worked with arrays which, as we know, are collections of  elements  everyone  the  same  type,  located  on  memory  one  to  continuation  from  other;  the number of elements is fixed at the time of creating the array. If later,  during the execution of the program, we would need to modify its size so that  contains more or fewer elements, the only possible alternative would be to assign a  new memory space of the required size and additionally copy the data into it  that we need to keep from the original array. The new matrix will become  matrix  current  and  the  matrix  origin  I know  will destroy,  Yes  already  no  outside  necessary.

Is  evident  what  every  time  what  we need  Add  or  remove  a  element  to  a collection of elements, the solution proposed in the previous paragraph is not the  most suitable; sure that we are thinking of some mechanism that allows us  add a single item to the collection, or remove it. This mechanism is  viable if instead of working with arrays we do it with linear lists. A list  linear is an originally empty collection of elements of any type not  necessarily consecutive in memory, which during the execution of the program  can grow or decrease element by element according to the needs foreseen in the  same.

According to the definition given, a question arises: if the elements are not consistent  tives in memory, how will we get from one element to the next when re-  let's run the list? The answer is that each element must store information  where the next or previous element is from, or both. In function of the  information that each element of the list stores regarding the location of  their predecessors and/or predecessors, the lists can be classified in: simple lists-  linked mind, circular lists, doubly linked lists and circular lists  doubly  linked.

### A  EXAMPLE WITH LINEAR LISTS

Based on the basic operations on linear lists described above,  We are now going to write an application that allows us to create a free list  simply linked neal ( llse ) in which each element consists of two members.  bros:  a  value  real  from  type  double  and  a  pointer  to  a  element  the  same  type.

typedef  structure  s

{

structure  s  *following;  //  pointer  to the  following  element

To create and manipulate the linear list, to a first approximation, we will  write the following functions: error , newElement , adddirToBeginning , mos-  fetchAll and deleteAll . This set of functions form what is called  interface: medium used by one object to communicate with another; for example, the  interface that we are now trying to write will be the medium that an application will use,  that we do later, to communicate with the linear list, in general with a  data structure. Why an interface? Because it is a way of reusing co-  say,  already  what  different  Applications  what  go  to  to work  with  a  determined  type

from  structure  from  data  they can  use  all  the  same  Interface;  evidently,  Yes  already  we have  from  her,  no  be  necessary  write it  from  new  for  every  application.

![](Images/image18766.jpeg)Interface

The newItem function will allocate memory for a new item from the  ready; when this is not possible, it will call the error function to notify it and  abort the program. The addadrToBeginning function will allow you to add a new  element at the beginning of the list, showAll will display on the screen  all items in the list and deleteAll will delete all items in the list.  ready  releasing  the  memory  assigned  for  every  one  from  they.

According to the above, the interface that we have referred to in the previous paragraph  rior  it will be like this:
