Based on this interface, we are going to write a ListaLinealSE application  create a single-linked linear list to store a series of values.  res of type  double  entered by the keyboard. Finally, to verify that all  ha  happened  What  we expected,  we will show  the  ready  from  values.

### Interface  generic  for  lists  linear

The interface implemented above has been designed to manipulate lists of  a specific type of elements: data of type  double  . This  is  the  address  on  the  what  we go  to  to work  next. In C this is done by using a generic pointer (  void *  ) to  point  to it  What have we  called area  of data.

### LISTS  CIRCULARS

A circular list is a linear list in which the last element points to the first.  river Then it is possible to access any element of the list from any  given point. Operations on a circular list are easier, since  special cases are avoided. For example, the anyadir function of the llse interface ex-  put above considers two cases: insert at the beginning of the list and insert  tar following an element. With a circular list, these two cases are  reduce to one. The figure below shows what a simple circular list looks like.  mind  linked.

![](Images/image18788.jpeg)latest

When  we travel  a  ready  circular,  we will say  what  we have  arrived  to the  final  from  the same when we meet again at the starting point, assuming,  of course, that the starting point is somehow saved in the list; by  example, with a fixed pointer to it. This pointer can be to the first element  of the list; can also be to the last element, in which case it is also known  Choose the address of the first element. Another possible solution would be to put an ele-  special item identifiable in each circular list as the place of departure. East  special element is called the head element of the list. This pre-  sit,  what's more,  the  advantage  from  what  the  ready  circular  no  will be  never  empty.

As an example, let's build a circular list with a fixed pointer to the last  thymus element. A circular list with a pointer to the last element is equivalent-  tea  to  a  ready  linear  straight  with  two  pointers,  one  to the  beginning  and  other  to the  final.

To build a circular list, we will first have to define the type of the  objects that will be part of it. For example, each element of the list  can be defined as a data structure with two members: a pointer to the  next element and one to the data area. The data area can be of a type  predefined or of a user-defined type. According to this, the type of each ele-  mint  from  the  list can  come  definite  of the  shape  following:

typedef  structure  s

{

void  *fact; //  area  from  data

structure  s  *following;  //  pointer  to the  following  element

}  Element;

We see that because it is a simply linked linear list, even if it is  circular, the structure of its elements does not vary with respect to what was studied before.  riorly.

We can automate the process of implementing a circular list by designing  an lcse interface ( Implementally Linked Circular List ) that groups the functions  necessary to create each element of the list, as well as to allow access to  the  themselves. This interface will allow us later to obtain other interfaces  that they be more specific; for example, an interface for manipulating stacks or an  Interface to manipulate queues . We will study these data structures a little  plus  go ahead.

### Interface  to manipulate an lcse

The functions of the lcse interface that we are going to implement below work  over a last pointer that will be  NULL  when the list is empty and when  do not, it will always point to its last element. This pointer, plus the number of  elements  from  the  ready,  they will be  defined  by  a  structure  from  type  tlcse :

typedef  structure

{

Element  *latest; //  point at  forever  to the  latest  element  int  numberOfElements;  //  number  from  elements  from  the  ready

}  tlcse;

### BATTERIES

On  her, adding or removing plates is always done from the top of the stack. East  type of lists is also called LIFO ( last in first out ) lists.  get in,  first out).

Push and pop operations on a stack are known in languages  assemblers like push and pop , respectively. The operation of removing an ele-  mint  from  the battery  suppress said  element  of the  same.

### queues

A queue is a linear list in which all inserts are made by one end.  mo from the list (from the end) and all deletes are done from the other end  (from the beginning). For example, a queue in a bank. This type of list receives also the name of FIFO lists ( first in first out - first in, first in  leave). This order is the only way to insert and retrieve an item from the queue.  A queue does not allow random access to a specific element. Keep in mind  what  the  operation  to take off  delete  the element  from  The tail.

To work with queues we can design an interface, derived from the interface  which we have designed to manipulate circular lists ( lcse ). According to this, a queue  will come  defined  by  a  variable  from  type  tcola  synonymous  from  tlcse :

### READY  DOUBLY  LINKED

In a doubly linked list, as opposed to a single linked list,  each element has information of where the subsequent element is located and the  previous item. This allows the list to be read in both directions. This type of list  tas is useful when inserting, deleting, and moving elements are opera-  frequent tions. A typical application is a word processor, where the  access  to  every  line  individual  I know  make  to  through  from  a  ready  doubly  linked.

Operations on a doubly linked list are usually performed  without any trouble. However, it is almost always much easier to manipulate  their relationship when there is a double bond between the last element and the  First, a structure called a circular doubly linked list .  For  move  on  a  ready  circular,  is  necessary  to stock  from  some  way  a reference point; for example, using a pointer to the last element of the  ready.

The next section shows how to build and manipulate a list  circular  doubly linked.

### Ready  circular  doubly  linked

A circular doubly linked list ( lcde ) is a collection of objects, each  one of which contains data or a pointer to the data, a pointer to the element  next in the collection and a pointer to the previous element. graphically you can  represent yourself  in the following way:

![](Images/image18804.jpeg)

To build such a list, we first need to define the type of  objects that will be part of it. For example, each element of the list  can be defined as a data structure with three members: a pointer to the  next item, one to the previous item, and one to the data area. The area of da-  tos can be of a predefined type or a user-defined type. According  this, the type of each element of the list can be defined as follows-  tea:

typedef  structure  s

{

void  *fact; //  area  from  data

struct s *previous;  // pointer to previous element  structure  s  *following;  //  pointer  to the  element  following

}  Element;

We can automate the process of implementing a doubly circular list  linked, designing an interface that provides the necessary functions to  create each element of the list, as well as to allow access to them. The  Interface  what  we design  to  continuation  it covers  these  objectives.

interface for  manipulate a  lcd

The interface functions that we are going to implement will work on the parameters  meters last , current , numberOfElements and position . The last parameter will be  a pointer that will be  NULL  when the list is empty and when not, it will point  always to its last element; current will point to the last element accessed; wildebeest-  mereOfElements  is  the  number  from  elements  what  have  the  ready  and  position  indicates

the  index  the  element  pointed  by  current .  This  suggests  define  a  structure  from  type  tlcde  that groups  all these  parameters:

typedef  structure

{

Element  *latest; // will always point to the last element  Element  *current;               //  point at  forever  to the  element  accessed  int  numberOfElements;  //  number  from  elements  from  the  ready

int  position; //  index  the  element  pointed  by  current

}  tlcde;

### TREES  PERFECTLY BALANCED BINARIES

A binary tree is perfectly balanced if, for every node, the number of  nodes in the left subtree and the number of nodes in the right subtree differ-  Ren  at most in one  Unit.

![](Images/image18823.jpeg)![](Images/image18824.jpeg)![](Images/image18825.jpeg)![](Images/image18826.jpeg)n=1  ![](Images/image18827.jpeg)

Trees  perfectly  balanced

As an example, consider the problem of building a tree perfectly  balanced with the values of the n nodes being pointers of type  void *  , which  will allow later to address objects of the type of data that we need in  every  case.

This can be easily done by distributing the nodes, as they are read, equi-  positively  to  the  left  and  to  the  right  from  every  node.  The  process  recursive  what  The following is the best way to perform this distribution. for a  given number n of nodes and where ni (nodes to the left) and nd (nodes to the right )  cha)  two integers, the  process is the  following:

1. Use  a  node  for  the  root.

2. generate  the  subtree  left  with  neither  =  no/2  nodes  using  the  same  ruler.

3. generate  the  subtree  right  with  na=  n–ni–1  nodes  using  the  same  ruler.

Each node in the tree consists of the following members: numberOfNodes ,  number of nodes in the tree that have this node as a root, data , data stored  two  on  the  node,  pointer  to the  subtree  left  and  pointer  to the  subtree  right .

typedef  structure  s

{

int  numberOfNodes; //  nodes  the  subtree  what  have  is  root  void  *data; //  area  from  data

structure  s  *left;  //  root  the  subtree  left  structure  s  *right; //  root  the  subtree  right

}

In C we can automate the process of implementing a custom binary tree.  perfectly balanced by designing an interface that provides the necessary functions  necessary to create each node of the tree, as well as to allow access to the  themselves.

The  function  findNode  is  recursive  and  have  five  parameters.  let's analyze  their  last three to see why they are passed by reference: the third, to be able to  return to the calling function a pointer to the data area; the fourth, to be able  return the position of the node where these data are and the fifth, so that all  executions of this function in progress can update the position of the node  current in process. With a  local variable to the function obviously we could not perform the function that  has *i (because it is local to the function, its value could not be altered by anyone  of executions in progress). 2. Write an application so that, using a stack, it simulates a ca-  peace of performing the operations of +, –, * and /. Most calculators accept  so the infix notation and a few, the postfix notation . In the latter, for  adding 10 and 20 we would first introduce 10, then 20 and finally the +. When  operands are entered, they are placed on a stack, and when the operand is entered,  rador,  I know  take out  two  operands  from  the  battery,  I know  calculate  the  result  and  I know  introduce  on  the  battery.  The  advantage  from  the  notation  postfix  is  what  expressions  complex  they can

easily evaluated without a lot of code. The calculator of the proposed example uses  will lyse  the notation  postfix .

From  shape  summarized,  the  Program  will perform  the  following  operations:

a) will read  a  fact,  operating  or  operator,  and  it  will store  on  the  variable  oper .

b) parse oper ; if it is an operand, it will push it on the stack and if it is  an operator, it will pop the last two operands off the stack, perform the operation  tion indicated by said operator and will put the result on the stack to be able to  use it  What  operating  on  a  possible  following  operation.

To carry out this application we will use the interfaces stack_queue and lcse reali-  discussed in this chapter, so in this exercise we will simply limit ourselves to  use them  without further explanation.

The  Program  full  I know  sample  to  continuation:

}

}

{

*p  =  d;

return  p;

}

int  getOperands(double  operand[],  tpile  *battery)

{

//  Get  the  two  operands  from  the  top  from  the  battery  double  *pdouble  =  NULL;

if  (stack->numberOfElements  <  two)

{

2 -  stack->numberOfElements);  return  0;

}

pdouble  =  (double  *) getFromStack(stack);  operand[0]  =  *pdouble;

pdouble  =  (double  *) getFromStack(stack);  operand[1]  =  *pdouble;

{

//  operating  stores  the  two  operands  double  operand[2];

//  Battery  empty  tstack stack;  startStack(&stack);

{

A process is said to be recursive if it is part of itself, that is, it is defined  ne depending on itself. Typical examples of recursion can be found  frequently in mathematical problems, in data structures and in many  others  problems.

Recursion is an extremely powerful process, but it consumes a lot of  resources, which is why we will analyze it carefully, to know when and  how to apply it From this analysis we will deduce that although a problem by definition  tion  be  recursive,  no  forever  be  the  method  from  solution  plus  suitable.

A  example  is  the  function  from  Ackermann,  to ,  the  which  is  defined  for  everyone  the  values  integers  non negative  m and  no of  the shape  following:

A(0,n)  =  n+1

A  process  on  the  what  is  Really  effective  Apply  the  recursion  is  the  trouble  of the towers of Hanoi . This problem consists of three vertical bars A , B and C and  n discs, of different sizes, initially stacked on the bar  to , in order  from  decreasing size.

![](Images/image18831.jpeg)

The goal is to move the disks from bar A to bar C while preserving their order,  under  the following rules:

1. I know  move to  alone  a  disk  every  time.

2. A  disk  no  can  stand  on  other  plus  small.

3. I know  will use  the  bar  B.  What  battery  assistant.

A  possible  solution  is  the  algorithm  recursive  what  I know  sample  to  continuation:

1. Move  n–1  discs  from  the  bar  TO  to  the  B.  (the  disk  n  is  the  the  background).

2. Move  the  disk  n  of the  A -bar  to the C ,  and

3. move  the n–1  discs  from  the  bar  B.  to  the C. _

summarizing  are  terms  on  a  frame  we obtain:

|  | no. | discs | origin | other  tower | destination |
| initially | n | TO | B. | C |
| 1 | n–1 | TO | C | B. |
| two | 1 | TO | B. | C |
| 3 | n–1 | B. | TO | C |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |

The  function  to  perform  be  move n  discs  from  origin  to  destination :

move(n_disks,  origin,  another tower,  destination);

The  pseudocode  for  East  Program  can  be  the  following:

<function  move(n_disks,  TO,  B.  C)>

IF  (n_disks  is  higher  what  0)  THEN  move(n_disks-1, A, C, B)  move(disk_n, A, B, C)  move(n_disks-1,  B.  TO,  c)

ENDIF

END  <function  move>

### ORDINATION  FROM  DATA

One of the most common and useful procedures in data processing is  their arrangement. It is considered to order the process of reorganizing a  given set of objects in a given sequence. The objective of this pro-  This process is generally to facilitate the search for one or more elements belonging to  to a set. Examples of ordered data are the lists of students enrolled  sides in a certain subject, census lists, alphabetical indices of books,  bros, phone books, etc. This means that many problems are  related in some way to the ordination process. That is why the or-  denation  is  a problem  important  to consider.

Sorting, both numeric and alphanumeric, follows the same rules  that we use in normal life. That is, a numerical data is greater  than another when its value is larger, and a character string is greater than  other  when  is after  by order  alphabetical.

We can group sorting methods into two categories: ordering of  arrays or internal sorting (when data is stored in internal memory) and  file sorting or external sorting (when the data is stored in memory)  would die  external; usually  on discs).

This section does not attempt to exhaustively analyze all methods of  ordering and see its benefits of efficiency, speed, etc. but simply  We will analyze from a practical point of view the most common methods for  ordination  of arrays  and of files.

### bubble method

There are many ways to sort data, but one of the best known is the sort-  tion  by the method of  the bubble.

Let us see next the algorithm corresponding to this method to or-  deduce a list from smallest to largest, assuming that the data to be sorted are al-  macerated  in a  matrix of  n elements:

1. We compare the first element with the second, the second with the third, the  third with the fourth, etc. When the result of a comparison is “ma-  yor que”, the values of the compared elements are exchanged. With this  we got  carry  the value  greater than  the  position  n .

2. We repeat point 1, now for the first n–1 elements of the list. With  this  we got  carry  the  value  higher  from  these  to  the  position  n–1 .

3. We repeat point 1, now for the first n–2 elements of the list and so on  successively.

4. Sorting will be finished when, by repeating the ith comparison process,  ration there has been no exchange or, in the worst case, after  from  repeat  the  process  from  comparison  described  n–1  times.

### Method  quicksort

quicksort sort method is generally considered to be the best  currently available sorting algorithm. The process followed by this al-  gorythm  is the following:

The optimal value would be the median (the  value that is less than or equal to the values corresponding to half of the  elements of the array and greater than or equal to the values corresponding to the  other half). This means that the exposed methods  to sort arrays can also be applied to sort files using  hoisting  random access.

Hashing algorithms are search methods, which provide a length of  small search and greater flexibility than other methods, such as be the binary search method that requires the elements of the array  be  organized.

By search length we mean the number of accesses that are necessary  make  on  a  matrix  for  find  the  element  wanted.

This search method allows, as basic operations, in addition to the  search for an element, insert a new element and delete an element  existing.

A code table is a set of characters where each character is assigned a  number used for its internal representation. Some languages like Java  use UNICODE to store and manipulate strings, and others like C use  ANSI or ASCII.

### UTILIZATION  FROM  CHARACTERS  ANSI  WITH  WINDOWS

ANSI  ( American  National  standards  Institute )  is  the  play  from  characters  most widely used standard for personal computers. As the ANSI standard only  uses a byte to represent a character, is limited to a maximum of 256  characters. Although it is suitable for English, it does not fully accept many other  Languages. For example, to type the character    in the Windows environment, hold  hold down the Alt key while typing 0177 on the numeric keypad (see the table of  codes  on the next page).
